name: Romantic Comedy
era: 1930s screwball roots; the modern form 1989-2005, revived on streaming
summary: Comedy whose real subject is the distance between two people. The look is warm and high-key (golden-hour exteriors, bright apartments, city landmarks) so nothing threatens, while the framing does the storytelling: early scenes stage the leads in wide 50/50 two-shots with clear negative space between them, singles are matched in size so neither wins the argument, and as feelings grow the gap closes, the lenses lengthen and the background softens. The realization gets a slow push-in; the reunion gets an orbit. Comic beats still play in a stable medium two-shot so the banter's rhythm is cut on the line, not on the camera.

editing: cut on the line for banter
hold on the reaction that betrays the crush
slow dissolve or music bridge into the reunion

rules.when: the leads are still apart (argument, rivalry, first meeting)
rules.then: stage them in a wider 50/50 two-shot with visible space between them and cover with matched-size singles
rules.why: the empty space is the obstacle made visible, and matched singles keep the contest equal so the audience roots for the pair, not for one side

rules.when: a character realizes they are in love
rules.then: give it a slow dolly-in on a single, ideally while the other person is busy or looking away
rules.why: the push isolates a private change the other character has not seen yet; the audience now knows more than the couple, which is what makes the third act ache

rules.then: close the gap inside one frame (tight two-shot, longer lens, slow arc) rather than cutting between singles
rules.why: putting both faces in the same shallow-focus frame is the visual payoff of every earlier gap

avoid.why: it signals threat or drama and fights the genre's safety; save darker light for the third-act breakup if at all

avoid.why: it quietly tells the audience who is right, which flattens the sparring that makes the pair fun

name: Multi-camera Sitcom
summary: Comedy staged like theatre on a three-wall set and covered simultaneously by three or four pedestal cameras, so a whole scene plays in real time in front of a live audience. Everything serves line delivery and reaction: flat, even, low-contrast light so any angle cuts to any other; eye-level angles from the audience side only; medium singles and two-shots; cuts that land on the punchline and then hold for the laugh. The camera never comments; timing is the star, and the editor builds it from the simultaneous angles after the fact.

editing: hold on the reaction for the laugh

rules.then: never place a camera on the fourth-wall side of the set; every angle comes from the audience side
rules.why: the set has no fourth wall and the audience sits there; this also makes the 180-degree line automatic, which is why the cameras can cut freely

rules.then: cut to the best reaction single or hold the two-shot; never cut in the middle of the line
rules.why: the laugh comes when a reaction confirms the joke; a mid-line cut steps on the actor's timing

rules.when: a physical gag or an entrance
rules.then: go to the wide master so setup and payoff are in one frame
rules.why: the joke is causal; the viewer must see the door open and the face it hits

recipes.why: Four simultaneous angles let the editor cut purely for timing, and matched eye-level singles keep the characters equal so the joke, not the camera, decides who wins each beat. The held reaction two-shot gives the audience permission and time to laugh.

name: Spaghetti Western
summary: A western rebuilt as ritual and opera. Wide Techniscope frames swing from extreme wide landscapes to extreme close-ups of eyes and hands with nothing in between, faces in the foreground share deep focus with figures far behind them, and time stretches until a glance becomes an event. Light is hard, white and overhead; skin is sweat and grime. The score is a character and often cues the cuts. Morality is mercenary, so the camera admires style and nerve rather than virtue, and violence arrives as a sudden release after long waiting.

editing: EWS straight to ECU with no medium bridge
sound: operatic score with whistles, choirs, electric guitar
exaggerated foley: spurs, wind, creaking signs

rules.then: show the whole arena in an extreme wide first, then jump directly to close-ups
rules.why: skipping the medium scales makes each cut a jolt and turns the duelists' faces into landscapes

rules.when: a character enters or is revealed
rules.then: use a face in the foreground with the new figure small and sharp in the background, both in focus
rules.why: deep-focus depth staging lets one frame hold threat and reaction at once, so the audience reads the power relation without a cut

rules.then: make it fast and clear, after a wait far longer than feels comfortable
rules.why: the genre's tension comes from elongated anticipation; a short release makes the wait feel earned

name: Film Noir
summary: Crime pictures shot as moral claustrophobia. Low-key chiaroscuro leaves most of the frame black; hard single sources throw venetian-blind bars and stair-rail shadows across faces like cages; streets are wet so they reflect what little light there is. Low angles show ceilings pressing down, and an occasional canted frame marks a world off its axis. The femme fatale gets a soft glamour key with a hard edge light, the hero gets hard side light that splits his face. A fatalistic first-person voiceover tells the audience the ending is already decided, so the style is about how, not whether, the trap closes.

editing: slow reveal of the face from shadow
sound: brooding orchestral score or lonely jazz

rules.then: use one hard motivated source (a desk lamp, a window, a streetlight through blinds) and let most of the frame fall to black
rules.why: darkness is the noir world's moral state; a single source leaves characters half-hidden, which reads as half-honest

rules.then: reveal her in a slower, softer, more glamorous key than anyone else, often from the legs or silhouette up
rules.why: the lighting seduces the audience along with the hero, so the later betrayal implicates the viewer too

rules.when: the hero is trapped or realizes the double-cross
rules.then: go low-angle with the ceiling in frame, or add bars of shadow across him
rules.why: architecture and shadow become the cage the plot is building

name: Neo-noir
summary: The moral logic of film noir, shot in color and in the present. The single hard source becomes neon, sodium-vapor and dashboard light; black-and-white contrast becomes a split between saturated hues (magenta and cyan, orange and teal) in deep shadow; rain stays, now reflecting color. Widescreen anamorphic glass adds horizontal flares and oval bokeh. Pacing is often slower and cooler than classic noir: long silent holds, a car interior as confessional, violence that arrives abruptly and is shown more frankly. Some branches move the darkness into harsh daylight, where corruption hides in plain sight.

color: magenta and cyan neon against black
sound: analog synth or pulsing electronic score

rules.then: motivate every source from a practical in the world (neon, streetlight, dashboard, TV) and let the color of that source define the shot
rules.why: neo-noir replaces black-and-white contrast with color contrast; colored motivated light keeps the darkness while making the city itself the mood

rules.then: hold longer than the dialogue needs, with minimal movement
rules.why: the stillness makes the later burst feel inevitable and shocking at the same time

name: Supernatural Horror (Haunting)
summary: Fear built from what the frame withholds. Wide-angle lenses on long hallways and doorways leave large dark negative space that the audience searches for a figure that may or may not be there. The camera stays locked off or creeps forward in slow push-ins that feel like being drawn toward something; cuts are delayed far past comfort. Light comes from cold practicals and a single motivated source, leaving pools of black. The scare, when it comes, is often small and in the background plane, and sound design (room tone, low drones, a creak) does as much work as the image.

color: crushed blacks with detail barely holding

rules.when: the character is alone in the space
rules.then: frame wide with large empty dark areas (doorways, corridor ends, the space behind them) and hold
rules.why: the audience scans the negative space for a threat on its own, so the fear is self-generated and much stronger than anything shown

rules.when: approaching a doorway or a dark room
rules.then: use a very slow, steady push-in rather than a cut
rules.why: a slow inexorable move feels like being pulled toward something; the slowness implies inevitability

rules.then: place it small and out of focus in the background plane while the character stays unaware in the foreground, and do not punctuate with a cut or a music sting
rules.why: an unannounced background reveal makes the viewer doubt what they saw and keeps checking every later frame

name: Mockumentary
era: 1984 onward on film; dominant TV comedy form 2001-2015
summary: Fiction shot with the grammar of observational documentary, so the camera is a character with limited knowledge. One operator handheld, available or practical light, zooms that hunt for the reaction after it has already started, eavesdropping through doorways and blinds, and off-center talking-head interviews in which subjects reveal what they hide from each other. The comedy comes from the gap between what people say in the confessional and what the camera catches them doing, and from glances to the lens that make the audience complicit. No score inside scenes; the silences are the joke.

editing: cut from a claim in the interview to footage that contradicts it
reaction glance to camera as the punchline
sound: radio-mic dialogue overheard from a distance

rules.then: the camera may only know what a documentary crew could know: no impossible angles, no coverage that anticipates action, no shots from inside private moments the crew could not reach
rules.why: the comedy depends on believing in the crew; one impossible angle breaks the fiction and the joke with it

rules.when: a character says something revealing or absurd
rules.then: find the reaction late with a snap zoom or a whip pan to the listener
rules.why: a reaction the camera arrives at slightly late feels caught rather than staged, which is what makes it funny

rules.then: frame the subject off-center on a third, looking just off lens at an unseen interviewer, on sticks
rules.why: the steady formal interview contrasts with the wobbly observed scenes, so the gap between self-image and behavior becomes visible

name: Modern Practical Action
summary: Action shot so the audience can read every blow. Performers do the stunts, so the camera can stay wide enough to show full bodies and real contact, and shots last long enough to prove it. Rapid cuts are survivable because the point of interest is kept near frame center from shot to shot, so the eye never hunts after a cut. Wide-to-normal lenses, minimal shake, stabilized tracking moves that stay with the fighter, and rhythm built from choreography rather than from the edit. Color is usually stylized and bold (neon, teal, sodium) but the geography is always clear.

color: bold motivated color (neon blue, magenta, sodium)
editing: cut on impact, not before it
keep the point of interest at center across cuts
longer takes to show the stunt is real
beat of stillness before each new attacker

rules.then: keep the action's point of interest at or near frame center in every shot
rules.why: the viewer's eye is already where the next shot's action is, so even half-second shots read instantly instead of forcing a search

rules.then: frame wide enough to include the full body and the contact, and hold through the move
rules.why: showing the whole move in one shot proves it is real, and that physical credibility is the genre's pleasure

rules.when: a fight changes direction or enters a new space
rules.then: re-establish geography with a wide before returning to closer shots
rules.why: the audience must know where the attackers and exits are to understand the tactics

name: Monumental Sci-fi
era: 1968 roots; the dominant blockbuster sci-fi look 2016-present
summary: Science fiction told through scale and silence. Tiny human figures stand in vast negative space against megastructures, dunes or fog; shapes read as silhouettes against haze rather than as detailed effects. The camera moves rarely and slowly (glacial push-ins, measured cranes), and cuts are few, so each image has time to register as an event. Palettes are restrained and nearly monochrome, light comes from one large diffuse or hard source, and sub-bass sound design replaces melody. Awe here is mixed with unease: the environment is indifferent to the people in it.

editing: cut from extreme scale to a human face

rules.when: introducing a structure, ship or landscape
rules.then: include a tiny human figure for scale and leave most of the frame empty
rules.why: scale only reads by comparison; the small figure lets the audience feel the size in their body instead of reading it as a number

rules.when: the reveal of the alien object or space
rules.then: hold the shot long and move the camera barely or not at all
rules.why: stillness and duration make the image feel real and heavy; fast moves turn it into a theme-park ride

rules.then: cut to a close-up of a face reacting in silence
rules.why: the face tells the audience how to feel about the scale: wonder mixed with fear

recipes.why: The fog withholds, the back-to-camera beat makes the audience wait with the character, and the long reveal with a tiny figure turns size into a physical sensation. Cutting to a silent face then names the emotion, and the slow upward tilt extends the sense of an object too big for a single frame.

avoid.why: speed shrinks scale; the genre needs time for images to be absorbed
monumentality comes from emptiness and restraint, not from more stuff

avoid.what: heroic score swells over the reveal
avoid.why: melodic cues tell the audience to feel triumph; sub-bass and silence keep the awe uneasy

name: Classical Western
summary: The western as American myth, filmed with dignity and order. Extreme wide landscapes with low horizons and towering skies make the frontier the hero, people ride as small figures across it, and doorways and porch frames separate home from wilderness. Characters are framed at eye level, often in cowboy shots that keep face and gun belt together, in harmonious balanced compositions with deep focus outdoors. The camera rarely moves; when it does, it pans with riders or dollies gently. Cutting is classical continuity and the meaning is communal: who is inside the frame (and the door) and who is left outside.

color: saturated Technicolor skies and red rock

rules.then: open on an extreme wide with a low horizon and the figures small against land and sky
rules.why: the landscape is the moral and physical test; letting it dominate tells the audience the frontier is bigger than any individual

rules.when: a character belongs to the community or is shut out from it
rules.then: frame them through a doorway, porch or window from the dark interior
rules.why: the doorway is the boundary between civilization and wilderness, so a frame within a frame states where each character stands

recipes.name: The doorway homecoming
recipes.beat: a family watches from a homestead as a rider returns across the plain

shots.subject: B

shots.subject: A

shots.purpose: two-shot at the threshold: B inside the doorway, A outside it
shots.subject: both
shots.composition: door frame splits the frame between them

recipes.why: The interior-to-plain doorway frame immediately divides home from wilderness, and the extreme wide makes the rider's journey feel earned by the land. Matched eye-level cowboy shots give both characters dignity, and the final threshold two-shot lets the audience see whether he will step inside without a word being said.

avoid.why: that is the Italian western's operatic grammar; the classical form stays at human distance
the genre's calm, balanced frames express a stable moral order
